## Desargues Involution Theorem

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Suppose cross ratios can be defined on a set $\mathscr{E}$. If a map $f:\mathscr{E}\to \mathscr{E}$ is a non-identity projective map and $f(f(X))=X$ for all $X\in \mathscr{E}$, then $f$ is called an **involution** on $\mathscr{E}$, and $(X,f(X))$ is called an **involution pair** of $f$.
:::

::: {#lem-12point1}
Let $f:\mathscr{E}\to \mathscr{E}$ be a projective map. If there exist $A\neq B$ such that $f(A)=B$ and $f(B)=A$, then $f$ is an involution.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Since $f$ preserves cross ratio,
$$
(A,B;X,f(X))=(B,A;f(X),f(f(X)))=(A,B;f(f(X)),f(X)).
$$
By @thm-6point4, $f(f(X))=X$ for all $X\in \mathscr{E}$.
:::

::: {#lem-12point2}
Let $\ell$ be a line. A map $f:\ell\to\ell$ is an involution if and only if $f$ is an inversion.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
If $f$ is an involution, set $P=f(\infty_{\ell})$, so $f(P)=\infty_{\ell}$. Then
$$
(P,\infty_{\ell};A,X)=(\infty_{\ell},P;f(A),f(X))=(P,\infty_{\ell};f(X),f(A)),
$$
which gives $PA/PX=Pf(X)/Pf(A)$; hence $f$ is the inversion centered at $P$ sending $A$ to $f(A)$.

Conversely, if $f$ is an inversion, it naturally preserves cross ratio (inversion with respect to the point at infinity is a reflection about a point).
:::

::: {#cor-12point1}
Let $f$ be an involution on a line $\ell$, and let $P$ not lie on $\ell$. Then all circles $(PXf(X))$ share a common radical axis as $X$ varies over $\ell$.
:::

::: {#lem-12point3}
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a conic section, and let $f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}$ be an involution. Then the line $Xf(X)$ passes through a fixed point.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Set $P=Af(A)\cap Bf(B)$, and let $XP$ meet $\mathcal{C}$ again at $Y$.

By @cor-8point6, projecting from $P$ to the second intersection with $\mathcal{C}$ preserves cross ratio, so
$$
(f(A),f(f(A));f(B),f(X))=(A,f(A);B,X)=(f(A),A;f(B),Y).
$$
Since $f(f(A))=A$, @thm-6point4 gives $f(X)=Y$; hence $XY=Xf(X)$ passes through the fixed point $P$.
:::

::: {#cor-12point2}
In @thm-10point5, for a projective map $f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}$, if $f$ is an involution then $Xf(X)$ passes through a fixed point; otherwise $Xf(X)$ belongs to the envelope of a conic section and $X\mapsto Xf(X)$ is a projective map.
:::

::: {#cor-12point3}
Projective maps preserve involution pairs: that is, if $\phi:\mathscr{E}\to \mathscr{F}$ is a projective map and $f$ is an involution on $E$, then $\phi\circ f\circ \phi^{-1}$ is an involution on $\mathscr{F}$.
:::

::: {#thm-12point1}
## Desargues Involution Theorem
Let $A,B,C,D$ lie on a conic section $\mathcal{C}$, and let a line $\ell$ meet $\mathcal{C}$ at $X$ and $Y$. Then the four point pairs
$$
(X,Y),\quad (\ell\cap AB,\ell\cap CD),\quad (\ell\cap AC,\ell\cap BD),\quad (\ell\cap AD,\ell\cap BC)
$$
are involution pairs of a common involution.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Projecting cross ratios gives
$$
(X,Y;\ell\cap AB,\ell\cap AC)\stackrel{A}{=}(X,Y;B,C)_{\mathcal{C}}\stackrel{D}{=}(X,Y;\ell\cap DB,\ell\cap DC),
$$
that is,
$$
(X,Y;\ell\cap AB,\ell\cap AC)=(Y,X;\ell\cap DC,\ell\cap DB).
$$
There exists an involution $f$ with $f(X)=Y$ and $f(\ell\cap AB)=\ell\cap DC$ (hence $f(Y)=X$). Thus
$$
(X,Y;\ell\cap AB,\ell\cap AC)=(Y,X;\ell\cap DC,f(\ell\cap AC)),
$$
so @thm-6point4 gives $f(\ell\cap AC)=\ell\cap DB$.

Hence $(X,Y)$, $(\ell\cap AB,\ell\cap CD)$, and $(\ell\cap AC,\ell\cap BD)$ are involution pairs of $f$, and the remaining pair follows analogously.
:::

::: {#thm-12point2}
## Dual of Desargues Involution Theorem (DDIT)
Let a conic section $\mathcal{C}$ touch the four sides of a complete quadrilateral $ABCD$, and set $E=AB\cap CD$ and $F=AD\cap BC$. If $P$ lies outside $\mathcal{C}$ and $PX,PY$ are tangent to $\mathcal{C}$, then $(PX,PY)$, $(PA,PC)$, $(PB,PD)$, and $(PE,PF)$ belong to a common involution.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This is the dual of @thm-12point1.
:::

::: {#lem-12point4}
Let the two common external tangents $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ to the circumcircle and the $A$-excircle meet $BC$ at $X$ and $Y$. Then $AX$ and $AY$ are isogonal lines.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $P=\ell_1\cap \ell_2$, and let the $A$-excircle touch $BC$ at $T$.

Applying @thm-12point2 to the $A$-excircle and its four tangents $\ell_1,\ell_2,BC,BC$ (regarding $BC\cap BC$ as the point of tangency $T$) and projecting from $A$, we see that $(AB,AC)$, $(AT,AP)$, and $(AX,AY)$ belong to a common involution.

Since $P$ is the exsimilicenter of the circumcircle and the $A$-excircle, and $A$ is the exsimilicenter of the incircle and the $A$-excircle, @thm-2point3 (Monge's Theorem) implies that $AP$ passes through the exsimilicenter $X(56)$ of the circumcircle and the incircle.

By @cor-5point5, $AX(56)$ and $AT$ are isogonal, so $(AB,AC)$ and $(AT,AP)$ belong to the involution given by reflection across the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$; hence $AX$ and $AY$ are isogonal lines.
:::

::: {#lem-12point5}
Let $P$ be a point, and let $X,Y,Z$ lie on $BC,CA,AB$, respectively, such that $AP\perp PX$, $BP\perp PY$, and $CP\perp PZ$. Then $X,Y,Z$ are collinear.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Notice that $(PA,PX)$, $(PB,PY)$, and $(PC,PZ)$ belong to a common involution (rotation by $90^{\circ}$).

Set $X'=YZ\cap BC$. Applying @thm-12point2 to the complete quadrilateral $YZBC$ and projecting from $P$ shows that $(PA,PX')$, $(PB,PY)$, and $(PC,PZ)$ belong to the same involution.

Hence $X=X'$, so $X,Y,Z$ are collinear.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The line containing $X,Y,Z$ in @lem-12point5 is called the **orthotransversal**.
:::

::: {#lem-12point6}
Given $P$ and $Q$ not lying on the sidelines of $\triangle ABC$, let $X$ be a point, and let $\ell_A$ be the line through $A$ such that $(AB,AC)$, $(AP,AQ)$, and $(AX,\ell_A)$ belong to a common involution. Defining $\ell_B$ and $\ell_C$ symmetrically, the lines $\ell_A$, $\ell_B$, and $\ell_C$ concur at a point $Y$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Set $P_A=AP\cap BC$, $Q_A=AQ\cap BC$, $X_A=AX\cap BC$, and $A_1=\ell_A\cap BC$.

Then $(B,C;P_A,X_A)=(C,B;Q_A,A_1)$, from which the ratio $BA_1/A_1C$ is determined.

The corresponding ratios on the other two sides follow analogously, so @thm-2point2 (Ceva's Theorem) implies that $\ell_A,\ell_B,\ell_C$ concur.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
In @lem-12point6, the map $X\mapsto Y$ is called the **isoconjugate** transformation sending $P$ to $Q$.
:::

::: {#cor-12point4}
The isoconjugate transformation sending $I$ to $I$ is the isogonal conjugate transformation, and the isoconjugate transformation sending $G$ to $G$ is the isotomic conjugate transformation.
:::

::: {#thm-12point3}
Given an isoconjugate transformation, it swaps lines $\ell$ not passing through any vertex of $\triangle ABC$ with conic sections $\mathcal{C}$ passing through $A,B,C$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $\phi$ be the isoconjugate transformation with $\phi(X)=Y$.

If $X$ lies on $\ell$, then $f:BY\mapsto BX\mapsto X\mapsto CX\mapsto CY$ is a projective map. By @thm-10point3, the locus of $BY\cap CY$ is a conic passing through $B,C$ (since $f(BC)\neq CB$), and analogously through $A$.

If $X$ lies on $\mathcal{C}$, then $g:BY\mapsto BX\mapsto X\mapsto CX\mapsto CY$ is a projective map. By @thm-10point3, the locus of $BY\cap CY$ is a line (since $g(BC)=CB$) not passing through any vertex.
:::

::: {#lem-12point7}
Let $\phi$ be the isoconjugate transformation sending $P$ to $P$. Then $\phi(X)=X$ if and only if $X$ is $P$ or a vertex of the anticevian triangle of $P$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Here $\phi$ maps the line $AX$ to itself, so
$$
A(B,C;P,X)=A(C,B;P,X)=A(B,C;X,P).
$$
Thus $A,X,P$ are collinear or $A(B,C;P,X)=-1$. Applying the same reasoning to the other two vertices and using @lem-6point3 shows that $X$ can only be $P$ or a vertex of the anticevian triangle of $P$.
:::

::: {#lem-12point8}
Let $\phi$ be the isoconjugate transformation sending $P$ to $P$. Then the line $P\phi(X)$ is tangent to $(ABCPX)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $P\phi(X)$ meet $(ABCPX)$ again at $Y$. By @thm-12point3, $\phi$ swaps $P\phi(X)$ and $(ABCPX)$.

Hence $\phi(Y)$ is the second intersection of $P\phi(X)$ with $(ABCPX)$, so $\phi(Y)=Y$.

By @lem-12point7, $Y$ is $P$ or a vertex of the anticevian triangle of $P$; since the vertices of the anticevian triangle lie on $AP,BP,CP$ and not on $(ABCPX)$, we must have $Y=P$.
:::

::: {#thm-12point4}
Given an isoconjugate transformation $\phi$, set $Z=XY\cap \phi(X)\phi(Y)$ and $Z'=X\phi(Y)\cap Y\phi(X)$. Then $\phi(Z)=Z'$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Applying @thm-12point2 to the complete quadrilateral $XY\phi(X)\phi(Y)$ and projecting from $A$ shows that $(AX,A\phi(X))$, $(AY,A\phi(Y))$, and $(AZ,AZ')$ belong to a common involution.

By definition, $(AZ,A\phi(Z))$ belongs to the same involution, and $A,Z',\phi(Z)$ are collinear; hence $Z'=\phi(Z)$.
:::

::: {#lem-12point9}
Suppose $P,P'$ and $Q,Q'$ are two pairs of isogonal conjugates, and set $R=PQ\cap P'Q'$. Then the pedal circles $\omega_P,\omega_Q,\omega_R$ of $P,Q,R$ are coaxial.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Set $R'=PQ'\cap P'Q$; by @thm-12point4, $R'$ is the isogonal conjugate of $R$.

Let $P_1,P_2,Q_1,Q_2,R_1,R_2$ be the projections of $P,P',Q,Q',R,R'$ onto $BC$.

Applying @thm-12point2 to the complete quadrilateral $PQP'Q'$ and projecting from $\infty_{\perp BC}$ onto $BC$ shows that $(P_1,P_2)$, $(Q_1,Q_2)$, and $(R_1,R_2)$ belong to a common involution.

By @lem-12point2, this involution is an inversion with center $A_1$. By @lem-3point18, $P_1,P_2$ lie on $\omega_P$, and similarly $A_1$ has equal power with respect to $\omega_P,\omega_Q,\omega_R$.

Analogously, there exist points $B_1$ on $CA$ and $C_1$ on $AB$ with equal power with respect to $\omega_P,\omega_Q,\omega_R$, so the three pedal circles are coaxial.
:::
